In reading the Great Canon and composing this *Dhāraṇī-vidhi*, one must receive the empowerment of the five wisdoms (*pañca-jñāna-abhiṣeka*) and succeed to the rank of *ācārya* before one may transmit it.
Should one fail to do so, one will incur calamity and retribution for oneself. This is the secret injunction bestowed by the World-Honored One upon Ānanda.

The Dharma taught by Śākyamuni is both manifest and esoteric. The manifest is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, while the esoteric pertains exclusively to the Mahāyāna.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (the root scripture) consists of one hundred thousand verses in eighteen assemblies; with the exception of these eighteen assemblies, all other scriptures belong to the manifest category.
Among them, the *Buddhabhāṣita-yamāntaka-kṣudra-preta-tāraka-dhāraṇī-sūtra* found in the present Tripitaka was translated by Amoghavajra. The Buddha...
The *Sūtra on the Dhāraṇī and Divine Mantra for Saving the Face-Burning Hungry Ghosts*, translated by Śikṣānanda, exists in two translations;
both contain only the mantra for transforming food. This sūtra belongs to the Exoteric Teachings (*Hīnayāna/Śrāvakayāna*).

Amoghavajra further translated the *Yogacaryābhūmi-śrī-saṃgraha-ananta-dhāraṇī-yamāntaka-vidhi-sūtra* (The Ritual Manual for the *Yamāntaka* Dhāraṇī of the Essential Yoga Collection for Saving Ānanda), which further employs the Esoteric Teachings (*Mantrayāna*).
The *Mahākaruṇā-śūnyatājñāna-tantra* states: "Yoga" has the meaning of "correspondence.

This means that all phenomena—belonging to the objects, practices, and fruits of all vehicles—are in correspondence. The characteristics of the Secret Mantra are as explained in the *Xianmi yuantong* (Complete Penetration of Exoteric and Esoteric Teachings).
The origins of the *bali* offering are as explained in this very scripture.
The ritual for the maṇḍala is explained in the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha-sūtra*. There are five families (*kula*) in the Great Maṇḍala.
First is the Buddha Family, with Vairocana Buddha as its presiding lord. Next is the Vajra Family, with Akṣobhya Buddha as its presiding lord. Next...
The Ratna Family: Ratnasambhava Buddha is the presiding deity of this family. Next is the Padma Family: Amitābha Buddha is the presiding deity of this family.
Next is the Karma Family: Amoghasiddhi Buddha is the presiding deity of this family. Furthermore, each of the five families has four great categories:
first, the Vajradhātu; second, Trailokyavijaya; third, Sarvārthasiddhi; and fourth, Sarvavid.
Furthermore, within each of the four categories, six maṇḍalas are established:
namely, the Great Maṇḍala (Mahā-maṇḍala), the Samaya Maṇḍala, the Dharma Maṇḍala, the Karma Maṇḍala, the Four-Seal Maṇḍala, and the Single-Seal Maṇḍala.

This explains the four types of maṇḍala rites, namely: pacification (śāntika), enrichment (pauṣṭika), subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa), and coercion (abhicāruka).

The present one is the rite of enrichment, which pertains to supramundane *siddhi*. The Sanskrit term is *maṇḍala*, or *maṇḍala* and so forth; its translated meaning is "altar" (*tan*). According to...
In the *Sahasrabhujasahasranetra-kalpa*, regarding the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Dharmacakrapravartana performed at the mere moment of forming the intention, it says:
"By placing the mudrā in the space before one's body, it immediately fills the entire realm of empty space and becomes a great maṇḍala.
By placing the mudrā upon the heart, one's own body immediately becomes a great maṇḍala. From this, one should know that a maṇḍala is not merely [a physical diagram].

The meaning of *maṇḍala* will be clarified further below. As for the fact that the ritual manual (*vidhi*) of this fundamental scripture refers to it as a *samaya-maṇḍala*, it is the initiation platform where precepts are conferred upon disciples and spirits.
In the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-śatapañcāśatikā-vyākhyā*, the Sanskrit term *samaya* contains four meanings; the fourth meaning states: *samaya* is also an alternative name for *maṇḍala*.

Therefore, among the six maṇḍalas, the second is called the Samaya-maṇḍala; its name and meaning are one and the same. In the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-saṃkṣipta-pāṭha-vidhi*, there are both painted-image maṇḍalas and mudrā-maṇḍalas;
this refers to the mudrā-maṇḍala. The mudrā-maṇḍala is also called the "Mind-Following Maṇḍala" (*Cittānugata-maṇḍala*), because it manifests in accordance with the mind. [The Thousand... (Note:

The Ācārya (National Preceptor Vajrabodhi) was a man from the Western Regions who personally received the Dharma from Ācārya Nāgabodhi. He arrived in China in the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty.
Wherever he went, he established maṇḍalas and performed consecration (*abhiṣeka*) rites; he was thus the first patriarch of the Ācāryas in this land.
According to the *Mahāyoga-tantrarāja*, he is a Bodhisattva at the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) on the tenth bhūmi;
alternatively, he may be a Bodhisattva on the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*). Therefore, in the *Vajra-mahātantra-ratnarāja-sūtra*, he is referred to as a Vajrācārya.
The *Yamāntaka-vidhi-sūtra* states: "If one desires to engage in practice, one should [proceed] from..."

The training of a Yoga Ācārya consists of generating the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta, receiving the samaya precepts, entering the great maṇḍala, and obtaining empowerment; only then is one permitted to receive it.
Having received the five wisdom empowerments of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana and succeeded to the rank of Ācārya, one may then transmit the teachings. Otherwise, [it is not permitted].
They do not permit one another [to practice]. Even if one were to practice in such a manner, it would invite calamity and misfortune for oneself;
it constitutes the offense of stealing the Dharma, and ultimately yields no efficacy. The *Vidyādharapiṭaka-vidhi-sūtra* states:

"If a practitioner wishes to cultivate various methods of accomplishment (*siddhi*), they must first cultivate contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*) and the various mudrās, ensuring that all are mastered with precision and without error."
Error. If, at the time of performing the ritual, one has even the slightest doubt or error, the mudrā will not be accomplished;
consequently, the worthy ones and sages will not be pleased, and whatever one prays for will not achieve fulfillment.
The *Bodhicittotpāda-rakṣā-deśa-rāja-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states: "One should contemplate this body as being formed of adamantine solidity and indestructibility.
One should then assume the adamantine full-lotus posture with the body and, with firm wisdom, clearly contemplate one's own mind."
One should visualize a lunar disc at the tip of the nose, preventing it from wandering or dispersing.
It is pure and perfect, its color like solidified snow, cow’s milk, or crystal. This lunar disc is the bodhicitta;

though this bodhicitta is fundamentally without color or form, for the sake of sentient beings who have not yet attained realization, it is described as being like a lunar disc. — *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra)

The *Rājavidhi* states: When one seeks the self-mind and finds it ultimately unobtainable, one is then able to awaken to and enter the wisdom of the emptiness of persons and the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena.
One then contemplates this mind of non-apprehension as perfectly luminous, pure, and free from the obscuration of dust.
Like the full moon in autumn, it manifests radiantly upon the body and is revered by the mind-king (*cittarāja*). This is the fundamentally pure Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
In the *Buddhabhāṣita-yogamahātantrarāja-sūtra*, in the chapter on the Contemplation of the Bodhicitta of Great Wisdom, the Buddha said:
"This bodhicitta is itself the physical form (*kāyalakṣaṇa*); the nature of this physical form is emptiness, which is true bodhi."
Since the body is without distinction, the characteristics of speech are likewise so. The *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra* states: "First, realize the purity of the single path;
next, realize bodhicitta. Regarding the explanation of bodhicitta: "Bodhicitta is free from all natures and is not the five aggregates," and so forth, up to:
"Once one has personally awakened to bodhicitta and contemplated oneself as it truly is, one then generates [the resolve]."
The mind of great compassion causes all sentient beings to realize and awaken to the phenomena of their own minds as they truly are;
this is called the root of all, the supreme bodhicitta.
The syllable-seeds of the thirty-seven deities are to be visualized by the ācārya,
as fully described in the *Buddhabhāṣita-yogamahārājatantra* and the *Buddhabhāṣita-sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha-pratyakṣasamādhi-sūtra*. [This concludes] the first subjugation.

The *Sarvalokamahāmaṇḍalavidhi* states: At that time, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana entered the Vajradharma-samādhi of all Tathāgatas and gave rise to the empowerment of the Lotus Samādhi (*padmasamādhi*).
Having spoken this Samādhi of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas, the Heart of all Tathāgatas emerged from his own heart.
He spoke this Heart-mantra, saying: *Hrīḥ*. When he spoke this Heart-mantra, from the hearts of all Tathāgatas there appeared the form of a lotus, with countless colors and exquisite radiance.
Those rays of light circled back and forth, and from the Noble Avalokiteśvara...

The *Eighteen Assemblies’ Pointing to the Source* states: "Upon the lunar disc..."

There are mantra syllables arranged in a circle; fix the mind upon each individual syllable so that it accords with the principle of true reality (*dharmatā*). Having performed the practice, begin again.
[Then perform] the hand seal (*mudrā*).

In accordance with the *Vajraśekhara-saṃkṣipta-pāṭha-vidhi*, the right hand corresponds to *śamatha* (calm abiding), and the left hand corresponds to *vipaśyanā* (insight). The ten fingers correspond to the *pāramitās*:

the right hand represents the perfections of morality (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); the left hand represents wisdom (*prajñā*), skillful means (*upāya*), vows (*praṇidhāna*), power (*bala*), and knowledge (*jñāna*).

This is because in the Western Regions, one faces east; since the right is honored and the left is inferior, [the perfections are assigned accordingly]. *The Ritual Manual of the Lotus Heart of Cintāmaṇicakra* (Ruyilun lianhua xin yigui)

'The secret seal-forms (*mudrā*) produced by the great wisdom of the three vajras—if a practitioner binds these seals according to the ritual rules while reciting, they can extinguish all karmic offenses and furthermore..."
By contemplating the ultimate truth, one immediately realizes unsurpassed enlightenment; how much more so for other matters of accomplishment?
Furthermore, relying upon this bodhicitta, visualize it as a lunar disc. Upon that lunar disc, visualize the syllable Oṃ as the Vajra Body.
Next, visualize the syllable Āḥ, which becomes the Vajra Speech. The syllable Hūṃ becomes the Vajra Mind.
Therefore, whenever forming a mudrā, one should first visualize these three *brahmī* syllables.
The fact that the diagrams of hand-mudrās all contain the three *brahmī* syllables—Oṃ, Āḥ, and Hūṃ—is precisely the application of this scriptural principle. Furthermore, it is said:
"All mudrās arise from the Vajra-palm, the Vajra-fist, and the Vajra-bind."

Now, those who wish to perform universal offerings for the sake of universal salvation should, with utmost sincerity and devotion, prepare the ritual site with strict purity.

Having prepared incense, flowers, food, drink, pure water, and other offerings according to their means, they should perform the bestowal during the hours of the Dog or the Pig. [For] the hungry ghosts...
One may receive food, and the donor shall obtain merit. If one lets the proper time pass, it is merely a waste of effort and provides no benefit for the matter at hand.
This is derived from the fundamental teachings and is not a mere personal view. Should there be those who now violate this, the local region will lack peace; this is precisely the fault thereof.
If you wish to understand this in full depth, please consult the subsequent commentary; the text therein provides a complete elucidation.

The Dharma Master Chengshan, Nei-heng Zhiquan, and the junior disciples of Xiuzhou,
Juche and Jixian, have compiled this work for the Great Jewel Flower King’s Throne,
which is universally protected and upheld by humans and devas; I now ascend to expound it here.
The moment the eyes behold it, the auspicious assembly of Bodhi is inaugurated;
the gate of nectar is opened. Orphaned spirits and sons of the Buddha descend and arrive; hearing the Dharma, they attend the fragrant feast.
They are utterly liberated from saṃsāra, and the darkness of the underworld is instantly dispelled.

Therefore, when clouds gather here, this fragrance does not descend from heaven; how could it belong to the earth? Before the two polarities were yet divided, its root and source filled the three realms;
once the single breath was first parted, its branches and leaves pervaded the ten directions, surpassing the brilliance of the sun and moon.
Seizing the exquisite beauty of mountains and rivers—this is precept, concentration, and wisdom; it is neither wood, nor fire, nor smoke. Gathered together, it resides within a single atom;

dispersed, it universally perfumes the entire Dharma-realm. Incense is burned within the burner specifically to offer worship to the eternally abiding Triple Gem, the myriad spirits of the ocean of lands, the ancestral masters of successive generations, all the holy multitudes, and every species as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Whether hidden or manifest, holy or ordinary, all rely upon this true incense to offer universal worship.
This cloud of incense forms a canopy over the Buddha’s face,
which is like the pure, full moon, and also like a thousand suns radiating brilliant light.
The circular halo shines universally throughout the ten directions; joy, renunciation, compassion, and kindness are all fully perfected.
Homage to the Triple Gem of the Buddhas, Dharmas, and Sanghas of the past, present, and future, which pervades all of empty space and the entire Dharma realm.
Ascending the Jewel Throne:
It is hereby understood that upon ascending this throne of the Yoga of the Exoteric and Esoteric, one practices the Six Perfections in unison.

One opens the gate of saving beings and benefiting life through the equal bestowal of the Three Kinds of Generosity. With a single mind profoundly tranquil, the entire body is the Great Compassionate King; as the three karmas respond, one is liberated.
The essence of both becomes the syllable *hrīḥ*. Indeed, it is thus: this is the cause and this is the fruit; they do not emerge apart from one's own mind.

Whether for self-benefit or the benefit of others, how could they concern anything else? One may transform a drop of water into the ghee and curd of a vast river, and change a tiny morsel of food [into sustenance].
Acting as a vessel for the great earth’s food, in a mere instant you universally relieve the hunger and emptiness of the entire Dharma realm;

in a brief moment, you bring benefit to as many beings in the preta realms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges. If you can understand it in this way, you must universally benefit all sentient capacities.
If this is still not clear, I cannot help but proclaim once more these wondrous verses:

The Way is such that every atom and every world-realm Is entirely interfused and harmonious; Though there be ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences, They are all penetrated by a single thread.
Lifting up the moon upon the coral branch— Its brilliant radiance shines forth, illuminating endlessly.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion (At the conclusion of the assembly’s recitation, the Master offers this prayer for the water).
Now, as for this water: these waters of eight virtues are naturally so from the very beginning. First, they wash away the dust and defilements of the karma of sentient beings;

then, they pervade the Flower Treasury World-realm of Vairocana. Within it, there is no place where one does not transcend the cycle of birth and death. Water does not wash water; it is the wondrous, ultimate Dharmakāya.

Therefore, it is doubly radiant and manifest; because it can purify body, speech, and mind, one thereby enters all maṇḍalas and attains the samaya of empowerment.
The Tang dynasty śramaṇa Huiri said:
"If there are those who have not yet entered the great maṇḍala altar under a preceptor (upādhyāya) or ācārya, they may simply take the Great Wheel Vidyārāja Vajra-mantra."
Recite twenty-one times, then enter the maṇḍala. Thereafter, perform all mantra rites; they shall all be accomplished.

It is further said: while reciting the secret mantra, perform this visualization: that throughout the entirety of space, pervading the Dharma-realm, all sentient beings within the three realms of birth and death and the six destinies may swiftly enter the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra Realm and become equal to Vajrasattva.
(Bodhisattva).

(The master’s seal and mantra may be understood accordingly). One should visualize that in the space before oneself, at a height of seven to eight cubits from the body, there appears a golden syllable *bhrūṃ*.
This transforms into a sublime and wondrous palace, [as vast as] a great trichiliocosm.

These are combined into a single land. This land is then fused into a single palace, with each and every adornment exactly as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, consisting of supreme, wondrous, and joyful things. Question: These great trichiliocosm lands are combined into one;
how are they combined? Answer: All lands are by nature empty and quiescent. Who establishes boundaries? If one is free from the perception of sentient beings, [the lands merge].

Thus, the lands are inherently one. Question: Where are the sentient beings of this land placed? Answer: Sentient beings within [this land] are precisely the sentient beings within the minds of all Buddhas;
they share the same enjoyment as the Buddhas, so what further need is there to place them elsewhere?
Question: How can a palace be formed entirely by relying on mental conceptions? Answer: Those great chiliocosm lands and the like are all manifestations of the wondrously luminous true mind.
If separated from the true mind, they ultimately do not exist at all, for they entirely depend upon the power of illusory transformation.
Furthermore, the great trichiliocosm is taken as one's palace; thus, the myriad dharmas are governed by the self.
I take refuge in the Teachers, the Tamer of Beings, throughout the ten directions, Who proclaim the pure and subtle Dharma;
And the Sangha of liberation through the three vehicles and four fruits— May you grant your compassion and descend upon this Dharma assembly.
[Invocation of the Triple Gem] (The表白 [表白者] harmonizes with the incense and flowers; the incense and flowers are welcomed; the Acharya takes up the censer and makes the three invocations).
Homage! With single-minded devotion, we respectfully invite all Buddhas, Dharma, and Sangha; Vajrapāṇi and the Secret Lords; the Dharma-protecting Śakra-rāja and other divine kings;

the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others; the Brahmin seers; and the entire assembly of holy ones throughout the ten directions, pervading the entire Dharmadhātu within lands as numerous as motes of dust.
We pray that you will not fail your original vows, but out of compassion for sentient beings, grace this Dharma assembly with your presence at this very hour tonight.
(These lines regarding "this night" and "at this time" do not appear in the ritual manuals or sūtras. These Three Jewels and others belong to the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation) realm;
as they are about to descend to transform and guide beings, they are specifically invited. Having finished the invitation, the Ācārya joins his palms and says:)

Relying respectfully upon the Yoga teachings, I construct this maṇḍala; I pray that the Honored Ones of the Triple Gem, out of compassion, will graciously accept it and manifest the seal of the ritual procedures for the altar.
(The *Sādhana of the Thousand Hands and Eyes* states: Form vajra-fists with both hands, hook the fingers of the giving and wisdom hands together, and move them slightly at the chest.)
Recite the mantra:
Oṃ vajracaṅkrama hūṃ phaṭ ḥ. (The mudrā and mantra may be understood as before.
One should visualize the syllable at the heart center.)
Various rays of light were emitted, reaching as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven,
where they summoned the Wisdom Avalokiteśvara to enter the maṇḍala.
This Wisdom Avalokiteśvara then emitted immeasurable light and summoned [all beings].
I request all the Three Jewels, as well as the protective deities of the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings, to come to this ritual arena in infinite, layered succession. Question:
In this teaching, it is said that the fruit is the principal and the cause is the attendant; now...
How can the cause be the principal and the fruit be the associate? Answer: There are two meanings to this.
First, the practitioner takes Avalokiteśvara as the matured object of focus; thus, they first accord with this object and subsequently accord with the objects of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara emits light to summon and invite all Buddhas, which is just like the practitioner summoning and inviting Avalokiteśvara. Now, one relies upon the invitation of Avalokiteśvara.
The Buddha is not the presiding master. Second, this Bodhisattva is the Tathāgata Vīryadevendraprabharāja (威德自在光明王) from a past life who has relinquished his position to deliver sentient beings;
thus, he is at the level of fruition (*phala*). Even if he were to serve as the presiding master, there would be no fault. The *Ritual for Constructing the Mandala* states:

"If there is no Buddha upon the mandala, one should form the Seal of Turning the Wheel of Dharma for those who have newly resolved their minds. When the seal is manifested, it constitutes the mandala."

Regarding the ritual procedures, the *Sādhana of the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara* states: "Form vajra-fists with both hands, and hook the thumbs (*tarjanī*) and middle fingers (*madhyamā*) together.
It further states: "This is the seal of the Bodhisattva Dharmacakrapravartaka; as soon as it is bound and one forms the intention, place the seal before the body.
Upon the altar, this immediately constitutes the Great Maṇḍala of Universal Subjugation of the Lotus Family. Thus, one establishes the seal.
Upon the heart center, one’s own body becomes a great maṇḍala. By touching the image of the deity and so forth with the mudrā, they all become a great maṇḍala.
Placing the mudrā in the space before one’s body, it immediately fills the realm of empty space and becomes a great maṇḍala.
Even if a practitioner should transgress the ritual, err in the three karmas, or violate the samaya precepts, by binding this mudrā, [all faults are purified].
By reciting the mantra and performing empowerment, all faults are eliminated and everything is brought to perfection. Thereafter, one should reverently present one’s sincere intent.
Arranging incense and flowers, a precious altar is established; The myriad Buddha-realms reside upon a single hair-tip.
The mind merges with the subtle principle, making the void seem small; The Way accords with True Suchness, making the Dharma-realm vast.
The marks and signs of excellence, compassion, and the full autumn moon; where the transformation body soars, the evening clouds gather thick.
Within the mass of incense smoke, I behold the manifested response: Śākyamuni Tathāgata, who contains the myriad phenomena within the ocean-seal, bears witness to my merit.
May Amitābha Tathāgata compassionately embrace and guide us;
may Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva secretly bestow his protective grace;
and may the Venerable Ānanda manifest expedient means to inaugurate the teaching.

Fragrant Cloud Canopy (At this point, having finished reciting the memorial text, either hold the hand-incense burner while the ritual master strikes the leading chime and chants the names of the Thirty-five Buddhas;
the tone should be harmonious and slow. Alternatively, use the bell and drum and join the assembly in reciting the Great Repentance).
The Confession Master.
*Yogācāra-Yamantaka-Śrāddha-Vṛtti-Saṃgraha* (Essential Compendium of Annotations on the Yoga Yamantaka Śrāddha), Volume One;
*Yogācāra-Yamantaka-Śrāddha-Vṛtti-Saṃgraha-Ritual* (Ritual Manual of the Essential Compendium of Annotations on the Yoga Yamantaka Śrāddha), Volume Two.
Compiled by the Dharma Master of the Tiao River, Ziruojingguan;
revised by the Dharma Master of Mount Cheng, Neihengzhiquan;
and reviewed by the junior disciples of Xiuzhou, Juche and Jixian. Recorded in this book.
Buddha Vairocana, by the power of your vows, pervades the entire realm of saṃsāra;
within all lands, you constantly turn the unsurpassed wheel.

(Recite the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* once. [Note: The Tibetan version does not contain the words "silently recite. The intent of reciting the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* is fully explained in the *Bhagavatī-prajñāpāramitā*. )
As clarified in the *Pāramitāmahāvidyā-bhāvanā-vidhi*,
one addresses all Buddhas of the ten directions, Prajñāpāramitā, Bodhisattvas, Vajradevas, and all other infinite noble beings of the paths of action: "I, [Name], now,
through great compassion and riding upon the spiritual power of the Buddhas, invoke those of the ten directions."

Throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, within the three miserable realms, the hells, and all evil destinies—among all hungry ghosts who have suffered from hunger and deprivation for kalpas across vast eons;

among the various offices of Yama, the celestial bureaus, and the earthly purgatories; among the officials of the dark paths of karma, the Brahmins, and the immortals; and among those who passed away long ago.
To the spirits of the vast wilderness, the devas of space, and their retinues;

to the various classes of ghosts and spirits—may all Buddhas, Prajñā Bodhisattvas, Vajra Devas, and immeasurable sages and worthies, as well as the paths of karma, deign to bestow their majestic radiance.
Increasing compassion and protective mindfulness, I universally pray for all throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space:

the officials of the celestial bureaus and the underworld, the judges of the paths of karma, the immeasurable hungry ghosts, my parents from past lives, long-deceased ancestors, Brahmin seers, and all those with whom I have karmic enmity.

Those who have been burdened by wealth, life, various species, and lineages—heterogeneous spirits and ghosts, each with their retinues—shall, by the power of the Tathāgata, certainly descend at this time;
they shall receive the supreme and wondrous flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, the pure nectar of immortality.
May food and drink be abundant, nourishing the field of the body. May merit and wisdom increase, and may the bodhicitta be awakened.

May one forever abandon wrong conduct, take refuge in the Triple Gem, practice great compassion, and benefit sentient beings. May one seek the unsurpassed path and not undergo the various evil fruits of suffering within saṃsāra.
May one always be born into noble families, be free from all fears, maintain constant physical purity, and realize the unsurpassed way.
With the mouth always pure, one realizes the Unsurpassed Way; with the mind always pure, one realizes the Unsurpassed Way.
I extend the five offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the lands of the ten directions, and to the infinite assembly of sages and worthies.
And all the deities of the paths of action, I pray that you, with great compassion, descend upon this dharma assembly to bestow your grace.
(Offer flowers, incense, lamps, ointments, fruit, and music. This is a slight offering.
(The Master recites the syllable *HŪṂ* while forming the mudrā. For the six goddesses, these represent the six perfections; visualize them as being accomplished as the offering.)
The syllables emerge as [the goddesses of] flowers, incense, lamps, ointments, fruits, and music. The Mother of the Gods has one face and four arms, emitting light.
Her upper two hands hold the mudrās of [flowers, incense, lamps, ointments, fruits, and music]; her lower two hands have their palms joined in the *cakrāñjali*. HŪṂ OṂ A HŪṂ OṂ A HŪṂ HRĪḤ.
With these offerings of flowers, incense, lamps, ointments, fruits, and music, I worship the Mother of the Gods. May the Buddha, out of compassion, graciously accept them.
Whatever various subtle [offerings]—flowers, incense, lamps, ointments, fruits, and music—have arisen from the nature of causes and conditions, I offer them to the Guru and the Triple Gem;
may you, out of compassion, graciously accept them. Oṃ sarvatathāgata-puṣpe dhūpe āloke gandhe naivedye śabde svāhā.
*Puccha-mi-khasamudra-spharaṇa-samaya āḥ hūṃ.* (The mudrā and mantra of the Master may be understood accordingly.
One should visualize the seed-syllable at the heart, from which six *hūṃ* syllables are produced, each possessing its own color and having the six *pāramitās* as their essence.
These transform into the six Ḍākinīs; they are of exquisite beauty and assume a posture of kneeling on the left.)
[They] perform a dance gesture to the right as an offering to the Buddhas. Question: What are the colors of the six [offerings]?

Answer: The flower is pale red; the incense is yellow; the lamp is crimson; the ointment is white; the fruit is reddish-yellow; the music is green-blue. This is because each corresponds to its respective color. Question:
How do these have the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) as their essence? Answer: There is a symbolic significance here. The flower symbolizes generosity (*dāna*). The cloth...
Generosity causes people to give rise to joy; incense represents ethical discipline (*śīla*), for when one maintains ethical discipline, one's karmic conduct becomes fragrant;
the lamp represents patience (*kṣānti*), for through patience, the fire of anger is transformed into great radiance; and the ointment represents diligence (*vīrya*).
Vigor represents the moistening of the *dharmakāya*. The fruit represents meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), for meditative concentration is able to bring the fruit of Buddhahood to fruition.
Bliss represents wisdom (*prajñā*), for wisdom is able to give birth to the various phenomena (*dharmas*). Question: Does this fruit possess these Mother Goddesses?
Or is it merely established based on the perception of their practice? Answer: These six Mother Goddesses are [contained] within the *Hevajra* (Joy-Vajra).
They are contained within the enclosure; all are Mothers of the Buddha, and all are the peers of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
The *Rucigarbha-padma-hṛdaya-vidhi* states: "Upon the moon disc at the heart, one visualizes the form of the syllable.
Having recited the syllable HŪṂ, it transforms into light of six colors. Within this light, they manifest as six Bodhisattvas, each holding [their respective implements]."
Regarding the offering substances: offer them universally to all Buddhas; first, present them to the Guru and the Three Jewels.

Recite the mantras for the five offerings and the music separately; these offerings are for the Three Jewels of the transformation field (nirmāṇakāya). The music and the five offerings are presented together (this differs from the previous case).
By the power of my Samantabhadra vows and practices, I offer flowers, incense, lamps, ointments, and food throughout as many buddha-fields as there are atoms, to all the noble sages therein;
I prostrate to each one individually and make offerings to them all.
Next, perform the mudrā for the mental offering of dedication.
namaḥ samantabhadraya candrasūryamukhaye oṃ sarva-...
Vṛttāntakadeśaspharaṇākramaṇakaṃ svāhā.

(The Susiddhikara Sūtra, in its section on the Ritual of Offerings, states: "Join the two hands with the palms facing outward and interlaced, placing the right hand over the left, and position them upon the crown of the head.
Whenever performing an offering, one should employ this method. With utmost sincerity and faith, present the argha water. )
All are accomplished through the recitation of mantras and the performance of mudrās, as well as by directing the mind and joining the palms up to the crown of the head;
only then is the method of perfect worship completed. Furthermore, it says: "Next, regarding the mental offering of worship:
one mentally visualizes flowers from both water and land, unclaimed by any owner, filling the entirety of space throughout the ten directions, as well as sublime ointments for humans and devas."
Fragrant clouds; burning incense, lamps, and light; banners, pennants, parasols, and canopies; various kinds of drums and music; singing, dancing, and performances;
nets of pearls; hanging precious bells; flower garlands and white fly-whisks; exquisite gongs and chimes; nets of *kaṅkani* pearls; wish-fulfilling jewel trees and garments;
celestial kitchens with all manner of food; sublime pavilions; and ornaments for adorning the body—the practitioner directs his mind toward these.
Pervading the entirety of space, such worship performed with a heart of utmost sincerity is the most supreme. The *Vajraśekhara-sūtra* (Dainichi-kyō Ryakushō Nenju Zuigyō-hō) states:
"Next, one should offer according to one's capacity as an expression of sincere devotion—consecrated water (*argha*), incense, food, and lamps, even down to a single flower or a drop of water;
or else, by merely directing the mind in visualization, the merit is exceptionally vast and immeasurable, whether expressed through material offerings or not."
[The mudrās] are simultaneous; all are accomplished at once. The *Vajraśekhara-yoga-japa-sūtra*, fascicle four, states:
"Next, the method for offering food and drink is explained. One should offer various kinds of fragrant, pure, and subtle delicacies.

If one is unable to provide these, one should perform the rite according to one's ability and then further contemplate in the mind: 'All the most excellent and sublime foods and drinks that exist in the world, as well as [all other varieties]..."
Various rare fruits such as grapes and pomegranates, and all kinds of non-seasonal juices—these I offer as an act of worship.
With a heart of utmost sincerity, I present this nectar-food; I pray that the Honored Ones of the Triple Gem will compassionately accept it with pity.
Next, form the seal for offering to the Buddha (formerly known as the seal for expelling māras).
Oṃ vajra-ākṣepa hūṃ. (The master’s seal and mantra may be understood accordingly. One should visualize the palms...)
In the center, there are red syllables.
The bases of the characters emit light that issues from three points, forming a fanning gesture that drives away the māras upon the food vessels. Question: [What is this?]
"What kind of māras are upon the eating vessels? He replied, "There are the obstructing māras such as those who feed on odors and those who obstruct the offering of food;
therefore, they are now being dispatched."
The Tibetan edition states: "When about to offer food as a gift to the Triple Gem, first form the three-pointed mudrā.

The *Ārya-ratnapaṭala-dhāraṇī-vidhi-sūtra* states: "The Buddha-offering mudrā: With the right hand, press the thumb against the nail of the little finger; the remaining three fingers are like a vajra.
Turn them upward and form the Buddha-offering mudrā."
Relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power and according to the instructions, I recite the secret mantra to empower the nectar-food,
transforming it so that it fills the entire realm of empty space.
Next, I form the Seal for Transforming Space (with both hands joined in *añjali* like a lotus bud, held upright before the chest while reciting the mantra).
Oṃ svabhāva-śuddhāḥ sarva-dharmāḥ svabhāva-śuddho ’haṃ. Oṃ āḥ hūṃ. (The mudrā and mantra may be understood accordingly.
One should visualize that both the food vessels and the food are entirely empty and quiescent. Thus, divide and sever the food. Much...
Because it is defiled by contact, it is now emptied and made utterly pure. Within that empty space, one should visualize three syllables *phraṃ*.
These syllables are all golden in color and transform into food vessels. Inside these food vessels, one visualizes a white syllable *oṃ*, which transforms into something supremely sublime.
As for food and drink, all shall consist of the flavors of *sarpis*,
milk, curd, parched grain flour, honey, and so forth. Silently and with pure mindfulness,
recite "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ" twenty-one times.
Having pervaded [all] and made it exceedingly vast,
one again recites *caḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ* and performs the mudrā,
visualizing that which has come forward...

Visualize the ocean-like assembly of the Three Jewels appearing with vivid clarity. Once again, extend the five offerings while reciting the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī*, the *Manasvī-dhāraṇī*, and other mantras.

Contemplate that the Three Jewels are bestowing their grace. Divide the first portion of the offering and present it to the Buddha and the Dharma; divide the second portion and present it to the Bodhisattvas and the noble Saṅgha;

and divide the final portion and present it to the protective deities of the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings. Having completed these offerings, thereafter perform the *kula* (the ritual of gathering).
(Recite while visualizing the flow of water):
With this nectar-food, I offer it to all the noble sages; Out of compassion for us, may you graciously accept it with loving-kindness.
Next, form the mudrā for offering food:
Oṃ ākarṣaya muḥ sarvataḥ tarpaṇān.
Aḍya-nutpanna oṃ a hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. (With both hands,
place the two palms forward.)

The sides [of the hands] touch one another. The sides of the tips of the two ring fingers touch each other. The two index fingers are slightly bent and pressed against the sides of the middle fingers.
The two thumbs are pressed against the sides of the index fingers. This resembles the gesture of cupping water.

One should imagine that all the sons of the Buddhas universally accept and enjoy [the offerings], giving rise to hearts of joy. When seeking manifest results, they will certainly grant permission. Thus, one widely welcomes the assembly of sages to enter.
[The altar]. One should immediately make offerings with incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, and so forth.
The verse for offering food:
"I now present this nectar-food, equal in measure to Mount Sumeru, unsurpassed."
With color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor pervading all of space, may the Guru and the Triple Gem compassionately accept this; next,
may the protectors of the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings and all sentient beings throughout the realm of phenomena partake until fully satiated,
giving rise to joy, and may they dispel obstructive spirits and grant peace.
On this auspicious day, may the patrons and their kin Eliminate calamities, gather merit, and enjoy long life;
May all their aspirations be fulfilled as they wish, And may there be auspiciousness at all times.
Praise to the Triple Gem!

To the World-Honored One, of great compassion and sublime adornment, Who possesses perfect clarity and omniscient wisdom, able to bestow blessings and insight as vast as the great ocean— To all such Tathāgatas, I pay homage.
The essential nature is fundamentally free from all desires; By practicing in accordance with this, one may escape the evil realms.
I pay homage to those who realize the most profound and mysterious principle;
I praise and bow to those who have attained the supreme liberation within the path of liberation among all sublime dharmas.
I pay homage to that great assembly who uphold the pure precepts, are worthy of veneration, and are born from the field of merit as the most excellent and wondrous.
(Verse on Entering Dhyāna-samādhi) At Potalaka, she constantly dwells in meditative absorption; Responding to conditions and manifesting her response, she reaches everywhere.
Seeking out sounds to rescue those in suffering and deliver the deluded masses, She is therefore named Avalokiteśvara.
Next, enter the meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of Avalokiteśvara.
(The above constitutes making offerings to the Triple Gem; this is a gateway for cultivating merit. If one possesses merit but lacks wisdom, one will fall into the causal cycle of humans and devas.
Now, if one practices this meditative concentration of Avalokiteśvara, one possesses wisdom. Having attained both merit and wisdom, one is then equal [to the Buddhas].)
[Having paid homage to] all Buddhas, one may then bring benefit to sentient beings within the dharma-realm. The attendant announces: "Next, enter the samādhi of Avalokiteśvara.
The Master enters into meditative concentration. The Rector recites a verse; its tone should be valued for being gentle, harmonious, clear, and resonant.

It must not be forceful or harsh, for fear of obstructing contemplative visualization. Nor should it resemble the ordinary voices of worldly children or women. One should thus enter into concentration.
At that time, close your eyes and clarify your mind. Visualize within your own body a perfect, pure whiteness, like the bright moon.

Upon this pure lunar disc at the heart, visualize the syllable Hrīḥ emitting great radiance. This syllable transforms into an eight-petaled lotus flower, upon which stands the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with distinct and clear marks and signs.
His left hand holds a lotus flower, and his right hand performs the gesture of opening a blossom.
Śrī made this reflection: "Within the bodies of all sentient beings lies this flower of awakening.
In the pure dharma-realm, unstained by afflictions, upon each of the eight petals of the lotus, a Tathāgata sits cross-legged in meditative absorption."

Facing Avalokiteśvara, with a circular halo encircling the neck and a body like the color of gold, radiant and brilliant—visualize this eight-petaled lotus gradually unfolding and expanding until its measure equals the void.
With this awakened flower, illuminate and touch the ocean-like assembly of Tathāgatas, and may it become a vast offering.
Those who are touched by the illumination of this awakened flower shall, regarding all their sufferings and afflictions...
One attains liberation, becoming equal to the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of a Bodhisattva. Then, one visualizes the lotus gradually contracting until its size is equal to one's own body.
One binds the mudrā and recites the mantra, empowering the four places. By this empowerment, the body is made firm—namely, the crown of the head, the throat, the heart, and the navel.
At each point of the mudrā, the syllable *hrīḥ* (dvi-svabhāva) is formed; these syllables are sealed by the two hands joined with the palms facing outward.
Form the *viśvavajra* mudrā: join the two index fingers together like lotus petals and hold the two thumbs side by side, upright.
Then recite the mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (the verse on the meditative concentration of Avalokiteśvara).
Homage to the inexhaustible Triple Gem! I now vow to generate the bodhicitta;
May the Bodhisattva come to accept and guide me, So that I may swiftly realize the subtle and wondrous body of Avalokiteśvara.
Next, enter the samādhi of Avalokiteśvara: With a tranquil mind, close your eyes and contemplate within the heart.
Upon a perfectly full, brilliant, and pure moon disc, The seed-syllable emits light, forming a lotus flower.
Within the flower is one Avalokiteśvara, Endowed with all the marks and signs, peerless and matchless.
His left hand holds a wondrous lotus flower, And his right hand makes the gesture of opening its petals.
The Bodhisattva contemplates that the bodies of sentient beings are each endowed with the pure *dharmadhātu* of awakening,
a lotus flower free from delusion and defilement;
upon its eight petals sits a Tathāgata in the cross-legged posture of meditative absorption, each facing toward Avalokiteśvara.
The neck is adorned with a circular halo and the body is golden; Its radiance shines brightly and brilliantly.
Next, visualize that the flower gradually unfolds and expands, Its magnitude pervading the entire realm of empty space.
Contemplate that this Flower of Awakening illuminates the Dharma-realm, Vast and expansive together with the ocean-like assembly of Tathāgatas.

Therefore, if the mind does not shift from this samādhi, And one awakens to all sentient beings with compassion, The flower of enlightenment, illuminated by this light, is freed from suffering; One then becomes equal to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
As the lotus gradually contracts to the size of one’s own body, One again forms the mudrā of the Sovereign Avalokiteśvara.
Empower the four places while reciting the secret mantra; Visualize yourself as equal to Avalokiteśvara.

By the supreme merit of this meditative concentration, Dedicate it to all sentient beings throughout the Dharmadhātu, That they may together behold Amitābha in the Western Quarter And fulfill the vast vows of Samantabhadra.
The mudrā of Avalokiteśvara’s meditative concentration:
Oṃ vajratara-ma-hṛīḥ. (Next, enter; treading upon what precedes, one follows what comes after.
This samādhi is the purification of the sensory objects through the clarification of the mind, which is the moment of purity.)
Furthermore, when the internal does not go out and the eyes are closed, that is the time for visualization.
When external conditions do not enter, [the mind is stilled].

"There is that which exists. [The Master] replied: "This clarifies the 'flesh-ball mind' (*māṃsa-piṇḍa-citta*).
